en: Oṃ! May my limbs, speech, breath, eye, ear, and likewise strength and all my senses, swell with vigor. May everything that is the Upaniṣad of Brahman be realized; may I not reject Brahman, nor may Brahman reject me. May there be no rejection, may there be non-rejection for me. May those virtues which reside in the self devoted to the Upaniṣads be in me; may they be in me.
Oṃ! I shall proclaim the *Vajrasūcī*, a treatise that pierces ignorance; it is a reproach for those devoid of knowledge and an ornament for those with the eye of wisdom. (1)

There are four castes—Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra—and among these castes, the Brāhmaṇa alone is the preeminent one; this is stated by the Smṛtis in accordance with the Vedic injunctions. In this regard, an objection arises: what indeed is a Brāhmaṇa? Is it the individual soul (jīva), the body, the birth (jāti), knowledge, action, or a virtuous character? || 2 ||

In this regard, if it is argued that the first [meaning] is that the living being (*jīva*) is a Brahmin, that is not so; because the living being remains of a single nature throughout many past and future bodies, because even for a single [living being], the occurrence of multiple bodies is possible through the power of karma, and because the living being is of a single nature across all bodies. Therefore, the living being is not a Brahmin. || 3 ||

If it is argued that the body is the Brāhmaṇa, that is not so. For, from the Cāṇḍāla down to all human beings, the body is uniform in nature as being composed of the five elements (*pañcabhautika*). Furthermore, one observes the equality of attributes such as old age, death, merit (*dharma*), and demerit (*adharma*) [in all]. There is no fixed rule that the Brāhmaṇa is white in color, the Kṣatriya red, the Vaiśya yellow, and the Śūdra black. Moreover, if the body were the Brāhmaṇa, sons and others would incur the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa (*brahmahatyā*) and so forth when cremating the bodies of their fathers and others. Therefore, the body is not the Brāhmaṇa. || 4 ||

If it is argued that one is a Brāhmaṇa by birth, that is not so; for among beings of other castes, there is the occurrence of many lineages, and there exist many great sages (*maharṣi*). For instance: Ṛṣyaśṛṅga was born from a doe; Kauśika from Kuśa grass; Jāmbūka from a jackal; Vālmīki from an anthill; Vyāsa in the daughter of a fisherman; Gautama from the back of a hare; Vasiṣṭha in Urvaśī; and Agastya was born in a water-jar, as is well known. Since these and many other sages established through their knowledge existed even without [specific] caste, therefore one is not a Brāhmaṇa by birth. || 5 ||

If it is argued that "a Brāhmaṇa is one who possesses knowledge," that is not so; for there are many Kṣatriyas and others who possess higher knowledge and perceive the ultimate truth. Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa is not defined by knowledge alone. || 6 ||

If it is argued that, therefore, action constitutes a *brāhmaṇa*, that is not so; for we observe that all living beings possess a commonality of *prārabdha* (commenced), *sañcita* (accumulated), and *āgāmin* (future) karma, and thus people perform actions being impelled by their karma. Therefore, action does not constitute a *brāhmaṇa*. || 7 ||
If it is argued that a Brāhmaṇa is therefore righteous, that is not so; for there are many Kṣatriyas and others who are givers of gold. Consequently, a Brāhmaṇa is not necessarily righteous. || 8 ||

In that case, who indeed is the one named Brahman? It is he who, having directly realized—as if seeing a myrobalan fruit in the palm of his hand—the Self as non-dual, devoid of genus, qualities, and actions, free from all defects such as the six waves and the six states of being, whose nature is existence, consciousness, bliss, and infinity, who is himself beyond conceptualization, who exists as the inner controller (antaryāmin) and the ultimate substratum of all conceptual constructions, who is woven like space both within and without, whose essence is indivisible bliss, who is immeasurable, known solely through direct experience, and manifesting in immediate presence; [having realized this, he is Brahman].

One who, having achieved his purpose, is free from defects such as desire and passion; who is endowed with tranquility, self-control, and other virtues; who is devoid of attachment to existence, envy, thirst, delusion, and the like; and whose mind is untouched by hypocrisy, egoism, and so forth—one who exists with these aforementioned characteristics is alone a *brāhmaṇa*. This is the intended meaning of the Śrutis, Smṛtis, Itihāsas, and Purāṇas. Otherwise, the attainment of the status of a *brāhmaṇa* does not exist at all. "One should meditate upon Brahman, the non-dual Self, which is Being-Consciousness-Bliss"—thus says the Upaniṣad. 9.

Oṃ! May my limbs, speech, breath, eye, ear, and likewise strength and all my senses flourish. May everything that is the Upaniṣad of Brahman be fulfilled. May I not reject Brahman; may Brahman not reject me. May there be no rejection; may there be non-rejection for me. May those virtues which reside in the self devoted to the Upaniṣads be in me; may they be in me.
May this be offered to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who dwells within the chief vital breath (mukhya-prāṇa) that is the delight of the Goddess of Speech (Bhāratī).
